passage: Sit, Pooja. You asked why your Vasudha Masi goes quiet in meetings even now. When I was twenty-four, my first boss at the insurance office was a Mr Kulkarni. Each morning, before I opened my mouth, I read his face: a loosened tie meant a good day; a file slammed on the desk meant say nothing. I had ideas, good ones, about the claims backlog. I wrote them in my diary and never said them aloud. When he asked, "Any objections?" I'd smile and say, "It's perfect, sir." Slowly I stopped even noticing my own opinions. I remember walking home feeling small, as if I'd shrunk an inch by evening. That habit stayed long after he retired. So when your manager asks what you think, tell her. Practise while it's cheap.

qa.q: What did a loosened tie mean to Vasudha?
qa.a: A loosened tie meant a good day.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel walking home in the evenings?
qa.a: Vasudha felt small, as if she'd shrunk an inch by evening, after hiding her views all day 😔

qa.q: What choice does Vasudha want Pooja to make that she did not?
qa.a: Vasudha wants Pooja to answer honestly when the manager asks for an opinion, practising while it's cheap, instead of learning to go quiet.

qa.q: What would change if Mr Kulkarni had welcomed objections?
qa.a: Vasudha's ideas on the claims backlog might have been heard, and she might not have carried the habit of silence for years.

grounding: An aunt recalls learning to read a powerful boss's moods, hide her views and shrink, as a young insurance employee.

passage: The slab had to be poured before the rain, and Hemant sir was in one of his moods. Raghav, twenty-four and eight months into the job, could tell from the way his boss chewed the pen cap: a fast chew meant anyone who spoke would be shouted at in front of the labourers. Raghav had spotted a sagging prop under the east corner of the shuttering. He rehearsed the sentence three times in his head. "Sir, the east corner..." Hemant turned. "What? Speak or move." "Nothing, sir. All ready." Raghav went and quietly wedged in an extra prop himself, hands shaking, as the first drops fell. The slab held. Nobody knew. That night on the bus Raghav realised he hadn't said one full sentence of his own all week.

qa.q: What did a fast chew on the pen cap mean?
qa.a: A fast chew meant anyone who spoke would be shouted at in front of the labourers.

qa.q: Why did Raghav say "Nothing, sir. All ready."?
qa.a: Raghav was afraid of being shouted at in front of the labourers, so fear of Hemant's mood swallowed the warning about the sagging prop.

qa.q: What went wrong at the key moment, and what could Raghav try next time?
qa.a: Raghav's warning died under Hemant's impatience; next time Raghav could lead with the plain fact, "The east corner prop is sagging," or tell another engineer so safety doesn't rest on one silent fix.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant asked the team for problems before a pour?
qa.a: Raghav could raise a sagging prop openly, and the site would not depend on a scared junior quietly fixing it in the rain.

grounding: Shows a junior engineer under deadline and rain reading a boss's moods and swallowing a warning, feeling he has lost his own voice.

passage: Every morning at the Andheri office, Kashish checked two things before logging in: the weather and Sachin's first message in the team chat. A cheerful "Morning, team!" meant she could ask for the leave she needed. A bare "Status?" meant keep your head down. Six months in, she had learned to rewrite her reports so the bad numbers sat at the bottom, softened. In meetings she waited to see which way Sachin leaned, then agreed. When he called her idea for the client deck "cute", she laughed along and deleted the slide. At home her flatmate asked what she thought about the new project. Kashish opened her mouth and found she didn't know anymore; she only knew what Sachin thought.

qa.q: What two things did Kashish check every morning before logging in?
qa.a: Kashish checked the weather and Sachin's first message in the team chat.

qa.q: What does Kashish's blank moment with her flatmate show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows Kashish has muted her own voice so long that she feels unsure of her own opinion and only knows Sachin's.

qa.q: What small choice could help Kashish get her own view back?
qa.a: Kashish could write down her own opinion before each meeting and keep one honest line about the bad numbers near the top of her reports.

qa.q: How might Sachin see Kashish, compared with what she actually thinks?
qa.a: Sachin probably sees an agreeable employee with no objections, not knowing her real ideas and doubts are hidden to please him.

grounding: Illustrates a junior employee watching a manager's moods, hiding her views and losing touch with her own opinions.

passage: "Naveen, you've been in front of that mirror for ten minutes." Suraj leaned on the bathroom door. "I'm practising. 'Sir, I have a small suggestion.' No. 'Sir, if you have a moment.' No." "For what?" "The client proposal. My numbers are better than his." "So tell him." Naveen laughed without humour. "You don't know Bhatia sir. If he comes in whistling, you can speak. If he takes his glasses off, you say, 'Yes sir, very good sir.'" "And today?" "Glasses off." "So you said nothing." "I said his plan was excellent." Suraj was quiet. "Bhaiya, at college you argued with the dean." "That was college." Naveen rinsed his face. "Now I just watch his glasses." "You've gone smaller," Suraj said. "Since you joined." Naveen looked at himself in the mirror and didn't answer.

qa.q: What does Bhatia sir do when Naveen should say only 'Yes sir'?
qa.a: He takes his glasses off.

qa.q: What does Naveen's rehearsing in the mirror suggest about how he feels at work?
qa.a: It suggests he feels nervous and watchful, so unsure of his boss's mood that he has to practise even a small suggestion.

qa.q: What small step could Naveen take with his better numbers?
qa.a: He could send the numbers in a short written note, so his idea is on record even on a 'glasses off' day.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the change in his older brother?
qa.a: Suraj sees that Naveen, who once argued with the dean, has become quieter and smaller since joining this job.

grounding: A young employee learns to read his boss's moods and say only what pleases, and his brother sees him shrinking.

passage: I'm Yamini. At twenty-four I got my first cook's job in Vaibhav Chef's restaurant kitchen, and I learned to read him before I learned his recipes. If he tied his apron twice round, the day was fine. If he came in with it hanging loose, nobody spoke unless spoken to. I had ideas. I thought the dal could use less cream, and I knew the order system wasted food. I said none of it. On good days he called me beti. When he asked, "Any problems?" I said, "No, Chef." I tasted my own cooking less and his mood more. After a year, a new girl asked me what I thought of the menu, and I opened my mouth and realised I didn't know. I'd been so busy watching the apron that I had stopped having opinions. I felt about half my size.

qa.q: What did it mean when Vaibhav Chef tied his apron twice round?
qa.a: It meant the day was fine.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel after a year in that kitchen, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt small and lost, since she could not answer the new girl's question and felt about half her size.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yamini, and what could she do next?
qa.a: Being asked her opinion and finding she had none showed her how much she had hidden; she could start by writing down one idea a week and sharing it on a good day.

qa.q: How might the new girl see Yamini when she cannot answer?
qa.a: The new girl might be surprised, expecting a cook with a year's experience to have clear views on the menu.

grounding: A young cook learns to read a powerful chef's moods and hide her views, and slowly feels smaller.

passage: In the Osaka office, Felix, twenty-four, had learnt to read Yuki's footsteps. Quick and heavy meant a bad morning; everyone kept their heads down. Slow meant she might be open to ideas. In meetings he watched her face before speaking. Once, early on, he'd pointed out a flaw in her plan, and she'd gone silent and cold for a week. Since then, when she asked, "Any thoughts?" Felix said, "It looks good." He had thoughts. He wrote them in a notebook he never showed anyone. At night, on the train home, he felt smaller than when he'd arrived in Japan: less funny, less sure. His friends back in Berlin asked why he never posted anymore. He didn't know how to explain that he'd forgotten what his own opinions sounded like out loud.

qa.q: What did quick and heavy footsteps mean?
qa.a: Quick and heavy meant a bad morning.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling on the train home?
qa.a: Felix felt small and unsure, less like himself after months of hiding his views.

qa.q: What small step could help Felix?
qa.a: Felix could share one idea at a time with a trusted colleague or through a written suggestion, rebuilding his voice without risking a big confrontation.

qa.q: How might Yuki see Felix's constant "It looks good"?
qa.a: Yuki may think he agrees with her and never realise how much he holds back out of fear.

grounding: A junior employee learns to read a powerful manager's moods and hide his views, and feels smaller for it.

passage: At the bank branch in Kanpur, the manager Yusuf-sir's cabin had glass walls, and every junior watched them. Sachin, twenty-five, had worked there a year. He knew that if Yusuf-sir tapped his pen, it was a bad day. If he loosened his tie, you could ask for leave. Sachin never said no in meetings. When Yusuf-sir proposed pushing a loan product that Sachin thought confused customers, Sachin nodded and said, "Very good idea, sir." At lunch, the other juniors whispered their real opinions, then went quiet when the cabin door opened. Sachin noticed he'd started talking less at home too. His wife asked why he seemed so quiet. He said he was tired. Really, he felt like he'd shrunk, and the only thing he'd grown was his ability to guess another man's mood.

qa.q: What did it mean if Yusuf-sir tapped his pen?
qa.a: It was a bad day.

qa.q: How was Sachin feeling when he said "Very good idea, sir"?
qa.a: Sachin felt uneasy and small, hiding his real doubts out of fear of the manager's reaction.

qa.q: What could help Sachin keep some voice at work?
qa.a: He could raise concerns in writing with facts about customer confusion, or find a fair senior he trusts to talk to.

qa.q: How might Sachin's wife see the change in him?
qa.a: His wife notices he has grown quiet and may feel worried or shut out, not knowing the cause.

grounding: A junior bank employee learns to read his manager's moods, hides his views and says only what pleases, and feels smaller.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,
You asked why I sound so flat on our calls. It's work. My manager at the agency is brilliant, and everyone's scared of her. I've learnt the signs: if she sighs before a meeting, don't pitch anything new. If she smiles, it's safe to ask for a day off. I plan my whole week around her face.
Last month I had a campaign idea I really believed in. I brought it up, she frowned, and I said "Or we could do it your way." I didn't even finish explaining.
The worst part isn't her. It's me. I used to argue with professors. Now I say "absolutely" twenty times a day. I feel smaller every month.
Can we talk on Sunday? Not about work. About what I used to be like.
Himani

qa.q: What does Himani say twenty times a day?
qa.a: Himani says "absolutely" twenty times a day.

qa.q: How does Himani feel about the change in Himani's own behaviour?
qa.a: Himani feels flat and diminished, more upset by Himani's own silence than by the manager.

qa.q: What could Himani do to reclaim some voice?
qa.a: Himani could talk things through with Jeevan, then try sharing one idea fully, perhaps in writing, rather than giving up before finishing.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jeevan might feel worried for Himani and eager to remind Himani of the confident person from before.

grounding: A junior employee learns to read a powerful manager's moods, hides personal views and feels smaller while saying only what pleases.

passage:
Parul, you asked why I've gone so quiet at work. I'm Tanvir, and here's how it happened.
In my first month I used to speak in meetings. Then one day I disagreed with my manager about a timeline. She didn't shout. She just stopped copying me on emails for a week.
Now I watch everything. If she comes in with her coffee, it's a good day. If she comes in without it, I keep my head down. I've learned to say "Yes, good idea" before she finishes a sentence.
Last week I had a better plan for the client, and I didn't mention it.
I feel smaller every month. I don't even recognise my own voice in meetings.

qa.q: What did the manager stop doing for a week?
qa.a: She stopped copying Tanvir on emails for a week.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel about not mentioning the better plan?
qa.a: Tanvir feels smaller and a little ashamed, having learned to hide views to stay safe.

qa.q: What small step could Tanvir try to get some voice back?
qa.a: Tanvir could share one idea in writing to the manager, or talk to a trusted senior about how to raise views safely.

qa.q: What would change if the manager welcomed disagreement?
qa.a: Tanvir would feel free to share the better plan, and the client and team might gain from it.

grounding: Shows a junior employee who has learned to read a powerful manager's moods and hide their views, feeling smaller as a result.

passage:
February: Damini joined the design team full of ideas. At her first review, she said Omkar's layout was too cramped. He said nothing. The next week her project was taken away.
April: Damini had learned his signals. A tap of the pen meant stop talking. A long sigh meant change the slide. She watched his face more than her work. When he asked, "Any thoughts?" she said, "It's perfect as it is."
June: A friend from college asked what she was designing. Damini opened her mouth and realised she didn't know what she thought any more. "Whatever Omkar wants," she said, and laughed. It didn't feel funny.

qa.q: What did a tap of Omkar's pen mean?
qa.a: A tap of the pen meant stop talking.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she said "Whatever Omkar wants" and laughed?
qa.a: She felt hollow and uneasy, realising she had lost touch with her own views.

qa.q: What could help Damini now?
qa.a: She could talk to someone she trusts, such as a mentor or HR, and start keeping her own design notes so her views aren't lost.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Damini's silence in reviews?
qa.a: Omkar may see it as agreement and not notice that she has stopped offering ideas.

grounding: Shows a junior employee learning to read a manager's signals, hiding her views to stay safe and feeling smaller over months.

passage:
Disha, you're scared of your new boss? Let your Abbu tell you about Sharma sahib. I'm Yusuf, and at twenty-four I was a junior accountant under him.
He could make the whole room silent by clearing his throat. I learned his moods like weather: a closed door meant storm, tea on his desk meant sunshine. I agreed with everything. I once changed a correct figure because he frowned at it.
One evening I went home and couldn't remember the last time I'd said what I thought. I felt like a shadow.
The next month I found an error in his report. My hands shook. I wrote it in a note, politely, and left it on his desk. He grunted. But he fixed it.

qa.q: What did a closed door mean in Yusuf's weather?
qa.a: A closed door meant storm.

qa.q: What did Yusuf feel on the evening he couldn't remember saying what he thought?
qa.a: He felt small and empty, like a shadow of himself.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Yusuf's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Leaving a polite note about the error; it let him use his voice in a safe way, and the boss fixed it.

qa.q: How might Sharma sahib have seen the note on his desk?
qa.a: He may have been surprised, but he grunted and fixed the error, which shows he could accept a respectful correction.

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a junior employee learning to read a powerful boss's moods and hide his views, and then finding a small safe voice.

passage: By month-end at the Mumbai firm, Santosh had learned to read Afreen Ma'am's moods from the corridor: fast heels meant trouble, silence meant worse. Today it was both, and the tax filing was due at six. When she asked if his draft was ready, he said, 'Almost, Ma'am,' though he thought her approach to one clause was wrong. He had tried disagreeing once in March; she had cut him off in front of the whole team, and he still remembered the heat in his face. So now he said only what pleased her. At 5:40 she found the error he had seen hours ago. 'Why didn't anyone flag this?' Santosh looked at his shoes. He had flagged it. In his head. He went home feeling a little smaller, as he had every month since March.

qa.q: When was the tax filing due?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel going home?
qa.a: Santosh felt small and discouraged, having hidden a concern he knew was right.

qa.q: What could Santosh try next time?
qa.a: Raise the concern early in writing, politely and with reasons, so it is on record without a face-to-face clash.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel on finding the error at 5:40?
qa.a: Afreen likely felt frustrated and alarmed, not realising her team was too afraid to flag problems.

grounding: Under a deadline a junior employee reads a powerful boss's moods, hides his view and feels smaller for it.

passage: At the Bengaluru agency everyone knew the rule: when Saurabh Sir walked in, you checked his face first. Yusuf, eight months into his first job, had learned it faster than most. If Saurabh was smiling, you could suggest an idea. If he was frowning, you nodded at whatever he said. Yusuf had a campaign idea he believed in, for the tea client, but he had never pitched it; the one time he spoke up in a meeting, Saurabh had said, 'Did I ask you?' Now Yusuf laughed at Saurabh's jokes a beat too early and praised slides he found weak. At home his flatmate asked what he had done at work. 'Agreed with people,' Yusuf said, and felt oddly tired, like a lamp turned down.

qa.q: What did Saurabh say when Yusuf spoke up in a meeting?
qa.a: 'Did I ask you?'

qa.q: How does Yusuf feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Yusuf feels oddly tired and diminished, like a lamp turned down.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do to share the campaign idea safely?
qa.a: He could write it up and send it when things are calm, or ask a supportive senior to review it first.

qa.q: What might Saurabh not realise about his team?
qa.a: Saurabh may not realise his moods make people hide ideas and agree falsely, so he loses good work.

grounding: A junior employee learns to read a powerful boss's moods, hides his ideas and feels diminished.

passage:
'You didn't say anything in the meeting,' Ujjwal whispered at the pantry. 'You told me yesterday the vendor plan was a disaster.'
'It is.' Indu stirred her tea. 'But did you see his face? The vein thing.'
'So?'
'So when the vein thing happens, I agree.'
'Since when are you like this? At college you argued with professors for fun.'
Indu was quiet. 'Since the review. He said I was not a team player because I questioned his numbers. In front of everyone.'
'So now you just smile?'
'I smile. I say "good point, Sir". I check his mood before I send any email.' She laughed, but it came out thin. 'I feel like I've shrunk a size.'
Ujjwal leaned on the counter. 'Want to send the vendor concerns together? Two names. Harder to brush off.'
Indu looked at him for a long moment. 'Maybe.'

qa.q: What did the boss call Indu at the review?
qa.a: Not a team player.

qa.q: How does Indu feel about how she has changed?
qa.a: Indu feels diminished and a little sad, as if shrunk a size, watching the boss's moods and hiding her views.

qa.q: Why might Ujjwal's idea of sending the concerns together help?
qa.a: Two names are harder to brush off and give Indu support, so she can raise a real problem without facing him alone.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see the change in Indu?
qa.a: Ujjwal is surprised and concerned, remembering how she argued with professors for fun at college.

grounding: A young employee under a powerful boss has become watchful and quiet, and a colleague offers to speak up together.

passage: The Holi week before the March closing was when I noticed how small I had become. By then I could read Bidisha ma'am's moods from the corridor: heels fast meant don't speak; phone face down meant maybe. I had a real doubt about the new vendor numbers. In my head I rehearsed saying it three times. In the meeting she asked, "All fine, Gautam?" and I heard myself say, "Yes, ma'am, all good." Everyone nodded. We all did that. At the office Holi lunch, colours everywhere, I laughed at her jokes a beat too early. On the bus home, pink powder still on my collar, I thought about the college Gautam who argued with professors for fun. I didn't know where that person had gone. I only knew I had got very good at being quiet.

qa.q: What did fast heels in the corridor mean to Gautam?
qa.a: Don't speak.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Gautam felt small and a little sad, missing the college self who argued for fun and seeing how watchful and quiet work had made that self.

qa.q: What small step could Gautam try about the vendor numbers?
qa.a: Gautam could write the doubt down with the figures and send it to Bidisha ma'am, which may be easier than saying it in a tense meeting.

qa.q: What might Bidisha ma'am be missing when everyone says "all good"?
qa.a: She might be missing real problems like the vendor numbers, because her team only tells her what pleases her.

grounding: A junior employee learns to read a powerful manager's moods and say only what pleases, and feels smaller for it.
